MESSAGE:
I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?

REQUESTS:
1. Suggest a name for the delivery van
2. Work out the drop order and timeline meeting all time windows, the break and the 12:00 return  KEY: Only feasible order is B -> A -> C. Leave 08:30, arrive B 08:50, unload to 09:05 (done before 09:30); arrive A 09:30, unload to 09:45 (inside 09:00-10:00); arrive C 10:25, wait until 11:00 (take the 30-min break during this wait); unload 11:00-11:15; back at depot 12:00 exactly (zero slack). A-first fails (B reached 09:40, after opening). Must give order B, A, C with a timeline that respects all constraints.
3. Rewrite the delivery text to be friendlier
4. List three furniture checks before handover
5. Recommend paper vs emailed delivery note
6. Define 'proof of delivery' in a line
7. Draft an evening-before arrival text under 160 characters

ANSWER:
The route works in only one order, and it brings the van back at exactly 12:00. Details first, then the rest.

## Tomorrow's route: B → A → C

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive B (20 min) |
| 08:50–09:05 | Unload at B. Done before the shop opens at 09:30 ✓ |
| 09:30 | Arrive A (25 min) |
| 09:30–09:45 | Unload at A. Within the 09:00–10:00 window ✓ |
| 10:25 | Arrive C (40 min) |
| 10:25–10:55 | **30-minute break** (waiting for C anyway) |
| 11:00–11:15 | Unload at C. Not before 11:00 ✓ |
| 12:00 | Back at depot (45 min) ✓ |

**Why this is the only order:**
- **B must come first:** if he goes to A first, he finishes at 09:15 at the earliest. The drive from A to B then gets him to B at 09:40, after the shop opens.
- **C must come last:** it can't take anything before 11:00, so it goes at the end.

**Two things to know:**
- **He returns at exactly 12:00, with no spare time.** C can't start before 11:00, and unloading plus the drive back takes exactly an hour. Any delay at C means he's late, however early he left. If 12:00 is a hard limit, ask office C whether they'll accept a slightly earlier delivery, or warn the depot he may be a few minutes late.
- **He must leave by 08:35.** The break fits in the wait before C only if he arrives there by 10:30. Leaving at 08:30 gives 5 minutes' leeway.

## Van name ideas

- **The Chesterfield**
- **Vanity Unit**
- **Dovetail**
- **The Restoration Wagon**
- **Sofa King Reliable**: check the staff will read it as innocent. It sounds a bit rude out loud, so drop it if in doubt.

## Friendlier "on the way" text

> Hi! Your driver is on the way and should be with you in about [X] minutes. See you soon!

## Three checks before handing furniture over

1. **Look for damage:** scratches, dents or chips from the journey, especially on corners and edges.
2. **Check it's complete and works:** doors, drawers and handles are all there, open properly and are secure.
3. **Check it's steady and clean:** it stands level without wobbling, and the packing, dust and fingerprints are gone.

Ideally, the customer looks too before signing.

## Paper or emailed delivery note?

**Emailed**, with the customer signing on a phone or tablet at the door. It's harder to lose, you have a timestamped record, and it's easy to resend. Keep a few paper notes in the van for customers who prefer them or when there's no signal.

## Proof of delivery

"Proof of delivery is the record, usually a signature, photo and time, showing the item was handed over to the customer in good condition."

## Evening-before text (under 160 characters)

> Hi [Name], your [Business] delivery is due tomorrow between [time] and [time]. We'll text when the driver is on the way. Any questions, just reply!

With a typical example, "Hi Sarah… Oakridge Restoration… 9:00 and 10:00", this comes to **153 characters**. The fixed wording plus times is 128 characters, so **name plus business name must stay under about 32 characters**. If your business name is long, cut "Any questions, just reply!", which saves 27 characters.

Two technical points:
- **Use a straight apostrophe** (') in "We'll", not a curly one (’). Some phones and systems insert curly ones automatically, and a single one can cut the message limit from 160 to 70 characters, splitting it into several texts.
- **No emojis**, for the same reason.
